technical_terms.how_marx_uses_it: The aim of capitalist production is the production of surplus-value, which the labourer must create for capital.
The capitalist buys the labourer's capacity to work, paying its value; the labourer's time beyond that is surplus.
The part of the working day beyond what the labourer needs to reproduce the value of his labour-power.
The part of the working day that produces the equivalent of the wages.
The power of labour to produce more in a given time, which Marx treats as a condition for surplus labour.
Surplus-value gained by lengthening the working day beyond necessary labour.
Surplus-value gained by shortening necessary labour through changes in production techniques.

technical_terms.term: formal and real subjection of labour to capital
technical_terms.how_marx_uses_it: Formal subjection means wage labour under capital's control; real subjection means capital controls the labour process itself.
The ratio of surplus labour to necessary labour, which can only be raised by lengthening the day or changing its parts.
Surplus-value divided by total capital advanced; Marx says it differs from the rate of surplus-value.
The part of capital exchanged for living labour-power, the transaction that capital hides.
The useful thing or quantity of goods a labourer receives, distinct from their value.
Labour is productive only as a social relation that creates surplus-value for capital.
Surplus labour is unpaid labour, because the capitalist gets it without an equivalent.
Workers combined in one process, each doing a part, so the product is social.
The process of labour as a man-nature relation, which Marx then studies in its capitalist form.
The output left over beyond what the producer needs, which Marx says is not inherent in labour.
Set by the value of the necessaries habitually consumed by the average labourer.

technical_terms.term: necessary labour time and working day length
technical_terms.how_marx_uses_it: Three factors fix surplus-value: working-day length, normal intensity, and productiveness of labour.
The average degree of expenditure of labour in a given time, which sets the value created by a working day.
Extra exhaustion from a longer day that can push the price of labour-power below its value.
The pool of unemployed or underemployed workers kept available to capital, which Marx calls a monstrosity.
The division that binds each worker to one detail operation, which modern industry sweeps away technically.
Production by machinery driven by mechanical power, which Marx sees as the typical successor to handicraft and manufacture.
Homework for capital, distinct from the old domestic industry; it is an outside department of the factory.
Machine-based production whose technical basis is revolutionary, in contrast to earlier conservative modes.
Labour of women, children and unskilled workers, which capital prefers as a basis for division of labour.
A fraction of the whole; surplus labour is always only a fraction of the day.
The capitalist's use of labour-power, spread over two periods.
The science that resolves each process into its constituent movements, which modern industry created.
